title: Strip 27 mm of insulation off a 35 mm² cable end with a round-cable stripping knife
instruction: Strip 27 mm of insulation off the free end of the cable with the cable knife.
context: Every conductor is stripped to length before it is terminated, so stripping is regular work for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS, wire strippers among their everyday tools; O*NET: "Connect wires to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components"). Feeders, sub-mains and earthing conductors of 16 mm² and more are past the range of stripping pliers (they stop at 16 mm²), so electricians cut their insulation round with a round-cable stripping knife whose blade depth is set to the insulation's thickness, here a JOKARI No. 27 SECURA, pressed onto the cable while it turns a full turn, and then take the cut piece off. Too short a strip and the 25 mm ferrule is not filled; too long and bare copper shows.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them (left positive). (1) A beech gauge block 150 x 50 mm and 16.5 mm tall, its long axis 60 degrees left of straight ahead, with a 12 mm hole 12.5 mm deep (its floor 4 mm above the table) whose axis is 30 cm forward and 7 cm left of the centre line, 25 mm from the block's front end. (2) A single-core cable of type H07V-K 1 x 35 mm2 (a class 5 flexible copper conductor 7.9 mm across under 1.2 mm of PVC insulation, 10.3 mm across overall, 340 g per metre), 10 cm long, its top 3 cm moulded into a square grey ABS plug 16 mm across, turned 45 degrees to the table's edges; 39.4 g in all (34.0 g of cable and 5.4 g of plug). It stands upright on its free end in the block's hole (0.85 mm of clearance all round). (3) A round-cable stripping knife, JOKARI No. 27 SECURA (part 10270; for round cables 8 to 28 mm across; 132 mm long, 29 mm wide, 35 mm high over its bracket, 72 g; a polyamide body with the blade in its front face, and a hardened band-steel bracket that closes a loop about 29 x 30 mm in front of the face), its blade set 1.2 mm out of the face, the thickness of the cable's insulation. It lies on its side on the table (its 29 mm width upright), the middle of its front face 39 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, pointing 60 degrees left of straight ahead. Lying on the block with the cable through its loop, the knife has its blade 27 mm above the hole's floor (14.5 mm above the block's top), so the block sets the strip length. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Pressed on: the knife's loop round the cable, its face pushing the cable with at least 6.0 N (the PVC's push back on the blade's 0.4 x 1.2 mm leading edge at its 12.5 N/mm2 flow stress) and its blade on the cable's insulated end. Cut all round: the cable turned at least 360 degrees against the pressed knife at one place along it (within 1.5 mm); that place's distance from the cable's end is the strip length. Pulled off: the conductor then drawn out of the knife (its end 2 mm past the blade) while the knife stays pressed on (at least 3 N), against the 25 N the cut insulation holds it with; if the knife is let off first, the cut insulation stays on the conductor. 1.0: pulled off with a strip of 25 to 29 mm (a 35 mm2 ferrule's 25 mm sleeve to its 29 mm maximum stripping length); 0.5: pulled off at another length, or cut all round 25 to 29 mm from the end but not pulled off; 0.25: the cable turned at least 90 degrees against the pressed knife at some point; else 0.0. In a real trial the stripped length is measured with a ruler or a caliper from the conductor's end to the insulation's cut edge (25 to 29 mm for 1.0); pulled off means the cut insulation is off the conductor (photograph); cut all round but not pulled off means it slides off by hand after the trial; the part-way cut, and the knife kept on while the cable comes out, are judged from the trial video. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the cable and the knife still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Take the cut insulation out of the gauge block's hole (or the knife), stand a fresh cable on its free end in the hole, plug up and turned 45 degrees, and lay the knife back on its side in its place, its blade depth unchanged (1.2 mm).
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz) at real size and mass; the cable is stiff and the knife is boxes at the maker's dimensions. Simplified: the blade is not a collider. Cut rule: while the knife's face pushes the cable with at least 6 N (contact force), each new degree the cable turns against it is resisted by 0.058 N m; 360 degrees cut it round. A joint to the gauge block, breaking at 25 N, holds the conductor in its cut insulation while the knife stays pressed.
